pool.prompt: What is the physical location, in a CO or hut, where an OSP engineer's responsibility for a fiber cable ends?
choices: The building wall, where conduit enters
The ODF/MDF splice organizer, where OSP fibers are broken out and spliced to inside-plant pigtails
The OLT port, once the patch cord is connected
The MEF primary protector
pool.explanation: The OSP termination point is the ODF splice organizer inside the MDF bay — where OSP feeder fibers are broken out and connected to inside-plant pigtails by fusion splice. This is the OSP/ISP boundary for the fiber path itself.

pool.prompt: In a fiber network, what does the MDF (Main Distribution Frame) typically take the form of, and why?
choices: A 66-block copper cross-connect, because copper is still used for cross-connects in fiber networks
An ODF (Optical Distribution Frame) — a rack with fusion-splice trays and connector panels, since the terminating medium is fiber
A CMTS chassis
A generator transfer panel
pool.explanation: An ODF is the fiber-specific equivalent of a traditional copper MDF, holding splice organizers and connector panels (LC, SC, MPO) instead of copper cross-connect blocks.

pool.prompt: An OSP engineer is designing feeder plant for a GPON FTTH network with an OLT rated Class B+. What is the maximum total optical loss the link can have from OLT port to subscriber ONT?
choices: 13 dB
20 dB
28 dB
35 dB
pool.explanation: GPON Class B+ (ITU-T G.984.2) sets a maximum 28 dB loss ceiling (with a 13 dB minimum) from OLT port to ONT. This budget must cover fiber attenuation, splitter loss, splice loss, and connector loss.

pool.prompt: Per ITU-T G.671, what is the standards-ceiling maximum insertion loss for a 1x32 PLC passive optical splitter, and why should this figure be used in link-budget design rather than typical field-measured values (roughly 17-17.5 dB)?
choices: 17.0 dB — always design to the field-typical value
18.1 dB — designing to this worst-case ceiling guarantees the link passes with any compliant installed splitter, even though real units often perform better
25.0 dB regardless of split ratio
There is no standardized ceiling
pool.explanation: ITU-T G.671 sets 18.1 dB as the compliance ceiling for a 1x32 PLC splitter. Designing to this worst case ensures the link passes even if the installed splitter is right at its allowed maximum, rather than optimistically assuming better-than-spec field performance.

pool.prompt: In a -48VDC CO power plant, which terminal of the battery string is grounded at 0 V (the battery return), under the negative-ground convention?
choices: The negative (-) terminal
The positive (+) terminal — the negative terminal drives the load at -48 V
Neither terminal — DC plants are floating/isolated from earth
Both terminals are grounded simultaneously
pool.explanation: Under the negative-ground convention, the battery's positive terminal is the grounded battery return (0 V); the negative terminal supplies the load at -48 V through the distribution bus.

pool.prompt: An OSP engineer is sizing a battery string for a rural hut. OLT load = 32 A. Required reserve = 4 hours. De-rating factor = 0.8. What is the required battery capacity?
choices: 128 Ah
160 Ah
80 Ah
pool.explanation: Raw Ah = 32 A x 4 h = 128 Ah. De-rating DIVIDES by the factor: 128 / 0.8 = 160 Ah. This accounts for high-temperature capacity loss and end-of-life degradation.

pool.prompt: What happens to CO equipment during the interval between utility failure and the generator reaching stable output?
choices: Equipment shuts down and restarts once the generator is running
The battery plant supplies DC continuously — no power interruption or reset occurs
A UPS bridges the gap using stored AC energy
The ATS momentarily disconnects all loads for safety
pool.explanation: The battery plant is a continuous, uninterrupted DC source. When utility fails, rectifiers stop and the batteries instantly supply the DC bus — equipment never sees an interruption. The generator's transfer time is entirely absorbed by battery reserve.
pool.citation: Standard telecom power-failure sequence; Telcordia GR-63-CORE [paywalled — general principle, exact transfer-time figure not independently verified this session].

pool.prompt: Per NFPA 110, a standby generator's monthly exercise requirement is:
choices: 10% of nameplate load for 10 minutes
At least 30% of nameplate kW for a minimum of 30 continuous minutes
100% load for 5 minutes
No load ('no-load run') for 1 hour
pool.explanation: NFPA 110 requires monthly exercise at no less than 30% of nameplate kW for a minimum of 30 continuous minutes. Running unloaded does not verify load-carrying capability.

pool.prompt: What is the primary risk of storing diesel generator fuel for more than roughly 12 months without treatment?
choices: Significant evaporation losses
Degradation — water absorption, microbial growth, and oxidation form gum, sludge, and sediment that clog fuel injectors
The fuel becomes a regulated hazardous waste after 12 months
The fuel becomes electrically conductive
pool.explanation: Stored diesel degrades via oxidation, water absorption, and microbial growth, forming contamination that can clog injectors and cause generator failure on demand. Fuel polishing or stabilizer treatment mitigates this.

pool.prompt: What is the ASHRAE-recommended thermal envelope for telecom/IT equipment inlet temperature (all A-class equipment)?
choices: 20-24°C only
pool.explanation: ASHRAE TC 9.9's recommended envelope is 18-27°C (64.4-80.6°F) for all A-class equipment. This is the recommended range for reliability/efficiency — the wider ALLOWABLE range (e.g., Class A2's 10-35°C) is a broader tolerance band, not the design target.

pool.prompt: A fire suppression system discharges a gaseous chemical agent (e.g., Novec 1230) into a CO equipment room. What happens to the OLT equipment after suppression and ventilation?
choices: Destroyed — gaseous agents are as damaging as water
Typically operational — clean agents leave no residue and cause no electrical shorts; a commissioning check verifies no heat/smoke damage
Must be replaced immediately as insurance policy
Requires connector lens cleaning due to agent residue bonding to ferrules
pool.explanation: Clean-agent suppression is specifically designed to avoid equipment damage — no residue, no electrical shorts. After ventilation and a smoke/heat-damage inspection, operations typically resume without equipment replacement.

pool.prompt: A lightning strike hits a pole 400 m from a rural hut. The feeder cable messenger is bonded to the MGN at every pole, and the hut has NO primary protector at building entry. What is the most likely outcome?
choices: No damage — fiber core is non-conductive
OLT line-card damage — the GPR transient travels via the bonded messenger and armor to the OLT chassis, destroying unprotected line cards
Minor, temporary signal interference only
Cable jacket rupture from thermal expansion
pool.explanation: The metallic messenger and armor (not the dielectric fiber core) form a GPR conduction path. Without a primary protector clamping the transient and bonding it to the GES, the surge routes through the armor into the OLT chassis.
pool.citation: RUS Bulletin 1751F-815 — Electrical Protection of Outside Plant.

pool.prompt: What does the IBT-entry (Intersystem Bonding Termination) accomplish at a CO building entry, per NEC Art. 250.94?
choices: Converts OSP cable metallic members to fiber-only
Provides a single accessible, listed bonding point where all incoming systems (power, telecom, cable TV) converge — preventing multiple separate ground points that create ground loops
Continuously measures ground resistance and auto-alarms
Connects the -48VDC power plant to the OSP cable's power feed
pool.explanation: NEC Art. 250.94 requires an accessible, listed device with capacity for at least three intersystem bonding conductors, giving all incoming systems a single common ground reference and preventing ground loops.

pool.prompt: Per TIA-607-D, what is the minimum TBB (Telecommunications Bonding Backbone) conductor size for a short backbone run, and what installation rule applies?
choices: #12 AWG; may be spliced at each floor
#6 AWG minimum, scaling up with length; must be a single continuous, non-spliced conductor
#2 AWG regardless of length; splicing permitted
No minimum size specified
pool.explanation: TIA-607-D specifies #6 AWG copper minimum, scaling to much larger conductors for longer runs, and the TBB must be a single continuous conductor with no splices, ensuring a consistent low-impedance ground reference.

pool.prompt: A CO building has its MEF 65 feet from the ODF rack. The OSP engineer wants to run gel-filled OSP feeder cable the full 65 feet before terminating. What NEC rule does this violate?
choices: NEC Art. 250.94 — IBT must be within 50 feet of building entry

NEC Art. 770.113 — unlisted OSP-grade fiber cable is permitted inside a building only for the first 50 feet from the point of entrance, and must then terminate in an enclosure or transition to listed cable
NEC Art. 230.70 — service entrance equipment location
No NEC rule applies to fiber cable length inside buildings
pool.explanation: NEC Art. 770.113 is the section that limits unlisted (OSP-grade) fiber cable to 50 feet inside a building before it must terminate in an enclosure or transition to listed inside-plant cable. (Note: Art. 770.26 covers a different topic — fire-spread prevention/firestopping — and should not be cited for the 50-foot rule.)

pool.prompt: Why is a trunk cable (pre-terminated MPO/MTP) preferred over individual pigtail splices for connections between adjacent ODF racks in a high-density CO?
choices: Trunk cables have lower loss than fusion splices

Trunk cables eliminate field splicing between racks — faster to install and more space-efficient, even though fusion splice loss (0.05-0.10 dB) is actually lower than MPO connector loss (roughly 0.5-1.0 dB per pair)
TIA-568 mandates trunk cables between any two adjacent racks
Trunk cables allow bidirectional signals on a single fiber, unlike splices
pool.explanation: Trunk cables are an installation-convenience and space-efficiency measure, not a loss-reduction measure — fusion splicing is actually lower-loss. The benefit is eliminating field splicing time and splice-organizer space between racks.

pool.prompt: A 72-fiber feeder cable serves FDH-1 (24 fibers, designated split) and FDH-2 (48 fibers, designated express) in a bus topology. A splicer accidentally splices fibers 1-24 as express instead of split. What is the result?
choices: No effect — the OLT reroutes automatically
FDH-1 is completely dark — fibers 1-24 now route to FDH-2 instead of FDH-1's splitters, so FDH-1's splitters receive no light
50% signal loss at FDH-1 only
FDH-2 is overloaded and fails
pool.explanation: Express vs. split is binary at the FOSC. Fibers spliced express when they should split never reach the intended FDH's splitters — resulting in complete loss of service for that FDH's subscribers until the splice error is found and corrected.

pool.prompt: Inside an FDH, what does a 1x32 splitter cassette do?
choices: Amplifies the optical signal for longer subscriber reach
Takes one feeder input fiber and passively splits its signal to 32 subscriber output fibers, with no electronics or power required
Converts the optical signal to electrical for local distribution
Filters wavelengths to separate video overlay from data
pool.explanation: A splitter cassette is entirely passive — a device made of fused fiber (or a PLC) that splits one input into multiple outputs with no electronics, no power supply, and no moving parts. A 1x32 splitter divides one feeder signal into 32 subscriber outputs.
pool.citation: ITU-T G.671 [confirm edition]; standard FDH internal architecture.

pool.prompt: Why are GPON subscriber ports at the FDH connector field always SC/APC rather than SC/UPC?
choices: SC/UPC is physically incompatible with FDH housings

The angled APC ferrule reduces back-reflection substantially versus a flat UPC connector; elevated back-reflection at one subscriber port can degrade upstream signal quality for all subscribers sharing that splitter
SC/APC is required for aesthetic/color-coding reasons only, with no technical basis
SC/APC carries higher optical power than SC/UPC
pool.explanation: Because a GPON splitter shares one feeder input across many subscribers, back-reflection at any single port can propagate upstream and degrade the entire shared PON branch. The angled APC ferrule minimizes this risk — the reason SC/APC is mandatory at GPON subscriber ports.

pool.prompt: You measured a fiber pair at 4.8 dB loss to the demarc during OSP handoff. A week later, ISP re-tests and reports 6.1 dB. Whose responsibility is it to investigate?
choices: ISP's — they caused it by patching
Yours (OSP) — a 1.3 dB shift is well outside normal OLTS measurement repeatability and indicates real degradation or contamination on the OSP side of the demarc
Neither — 1.3 dB is within normal measurement noise
The equipment manufacturer's
pool.explanation: A 1.3 dB shift exceeds normal OLTS repeatability (roughly +/-0.2 dB). The OSP engineer must inspect the fiber route, check the demarc connector, clean or repair as needed, and re-test to confirm resolution.
pool.citation: Standard OLTS repeatability practice; OSP/ISP handoff-boundary convention.

pool.prompt: ISP reports a fiber failed signal acceptance with RX power of -35 dBm (acceptable range roughly -28 to -5 dBm). Your OLTS baseline at handoff was 4.8 dB. What is the correct first diagnostic step?
choices: Ask ISP to re-test the fiber with OLTS at the demarc to compare against your 4.8 dB baseline
Order a replacement fiber immediately
Assume -35 dBm is within a different, undocumented acceptable range
Ask ISP to increase OLT receiver gain to compensate
pool.explanation: Re-testing at the demarc isolates the fault location. If ISP's re-test matches your 4.8 dB baseline, the fiber is fine and the problem is downstream (patch cable, port, or receiver). If it doesn't match, the fiber degraded and is OSP's responsibility.

pool.prompt: Match each element of the full OSP-to-ISP signal chain to the correct description.

items.label: OLT/headend — active equipment; ISP-owned; feeds the OSP feeder fiber
ODF/MDF — OSP/ISP boundary; OSP splices feeder to pigtails here
Feeder fiber — headend to FDH; pure OSP design and construction scope
FDH — passive splitter enclosure; clearest OSP/ISP demarcation point in most designs
Drop fiber — FDH connector field to ONT; last-mile OSP-installed segment
ONT — the demarc; carrier-owned up to its input, customer-owned beyond its output

pool.explanation: The full signal chain: OLT (headend, active, ISP) -> ODF/MDF (OSP/ISP boundary) -> feeder fiber (pure OSP) -> FDH (passive splitter, clearest OSP/ISP demarc) -> drop fiber (OSP-installed last segment) -> ONT (the demarc — carrier-owned to its input, customer-owned beyond).
